claims.text: Intentional aluminum addition and controlled thermomechanical processing induce a dual-phase microstructure in lightweight high-entropy alloys.
The induced dual-phase microstructure contains a low-density, aluminum-rich phase and a mechanically reinforcing second phase.
The dual-phase microstructure enables lower overall density than a homogeneous single-phase alloy.
The dual-phase microstructure enhances mechanical strength relative to a homogeneous single-phase alloy.
The dual-phase microstructure enhances corrosion resistance relative to a homogeneous single-phase alloy.
The dual-phase microstructure enhances high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to a homogeneous single-phase alloy.
High-entropy alloys synthesized without phase-specific tailoring typically exhibit a homogeneous single-phase microstructure.
Targeted thermomechanical treatments can promote formation of a dual-phase microstructure.
The aluminum-rich phase reduces the alloy's overall density.
The reinforcing phase provides mechanical strength.
The reinforcing phase creates diffusion barriers that improve corrosion resistance.
The reinforcing phase creates diffusion barriers that improve oxidation resistance.
Synergistic interaction between the aluminum-rich and reinforcing phases produces the enhanced overall performance.

Dual-phase samples will exhibit a measurable density reduction and statistically significant improvements in strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance relative to the single-phase baseline.
If composition or processing prevents formation of the dual-phase microstructure, the predicted mechanical and environmental-resistance improvements will cease to occur.

contradictions.description: The comparison is described as using identical or similar overall compositions, but only the dual-phase set receives controlled aluminum additions. Unless aluminum is correspondingly rebalanced in the baseline, the final compositions are not identical, so composition and phase structure are confounded.
